utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. Before the witness is brought in, I would like to make a short submission on the exhibits that I intend to use with this witness. As you may have seen, it's a quite extensive list of exhibits and I do not tend to tender all of them in the direct examination of course. The fact is that a number of these exhibits were not on the 65 ter list that we filed because we got them only afterwards. There are basically three groups of exhibits concerned. One group are documents that the witness handed over to us when we interviewed him in late August/early September last year; then there is a group of exhibits which are documents that we received in response to requests for assistance sent to Serbia and Montenegro, and they came dribbling in until early this year, January/February this year; and then there were two exhibits which I only saw last week because they were exhibits which were chosen in the VJ archive mission last year, that the translation was only coming back last week. And we disclosed the last two exhibits last week. The other two groups were disclosed at the time we received them, meaning the first group of documents that the witness brought in were disclosed in September when we -- when we informed the Defence that we would seek to add this witness to the witness list and the RFA responses were disclosed to the Defence I think in early January and the ones that came later on. So there has been notice of these exhibits. I would like to seek leave to add them to the exhibit list as we go along through them while the witness testifies today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The list that's attached to your weekly notification of the witnesses, does that contain all three categories of documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, and it contains a fourth one, namely those which were on the exhibit list because we were aware of them at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, how do we tell which ones were on the original list and which ones have been added? Is it clear when I look at this?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No it is not clear from the list, but I can mention it as I call up the exhibits and we can do it this way or I can also file something later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me find out what the response of the Defence is to this and then we can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have a principled objection to a group of documents. These are documents that were disclosed to the Prosecution in August when the witness gave his statement -- or actually, these were the documents we got from the witness at that time. The Prosecutor submitted a request to place this witness on the 65 ter list, as far as I can remember, on the 10th of November, 2006, and with the request there was no request for additional documents to be placed on the 65 ter list. So that is our principled objection to our -- to these documents. As for documents that were given to the Prosecution later, our Defence team feels that we have no objections to the documents regarding the deadline and the manner that the Prosecution is suggesting, but we do have another objection that relates to their relevance. And I would perhaps later state the objections. I do not want to overly complicate the situation at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. No one else wishes to comment -- Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I agree with my learned friend, Mr. Visnjic, but I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to note before the testimony of this witness begins to -- that exhibit 2672, I would like to draw your attention to that, it's the second on the list, it's the statement of the witness that he gave at the same time as he provided the statement to the Prosecution. However, this witness, in his signed statement, which is the first on the list in the last paragraph states that before providing the statement - this is paragraph 58 - he says, a review of the laws of the work of war prosecutions as well as the discipline and the duties of superior officers in the army drafted on the 14th of August I consider to be an integral part of this statement. So if we look at this a little bit better, which was drafted by the witness and which is an integral part of his statement, as he says, we can see that actually this is his expert opinion and comments on specific articles of specific laws. We agree that they are relevant, that they were in force during the critical period, but this witness is a factual witness; he's not an expert, even though he's our colleague and has passed the bar exam. In some parts, he's providing his opinion about the role of certain military organs and military officers, and I think before he begins his testimony, we would like to say that this exhibit should not be used during his examination-in-chief. As for other documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me an example from this one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the last part of this exhibit, the last subsection where he says, The duties, obligations, of senior officers of the army in the pre-trial and trial proceedings before those courts, and then in some paragraphs he says, The law on military courts does not say in what manner should the basic information be gathered. But then he gives his opinion, nevertheless, that on the basis of the law, you can know the basic way in which a military officer should react. A few paragraphs later he says -- he doesn't speak directly about the duties, but he says that it is the duty of a military officer to report a crime. And then the last paragraph before the signature speaks about a document which are instructions on the application of international laws of war. He explains some articles, and then in the last paragraph he says, This constitutes command responsibility and in a state of war the responsibility of a military officer with other regulations is also in force if he does not report the conduct of superiors to other organs. In our law, there was no term "command responsibility" and there was no specific crime of somebody being charged under command responsibility. So I believe that this last paragraph is an opinion provided by the witness and not his testimony on facts during the time that he was in Kosovo and worked at the military prosecutor's office during the time-period that is relevant under the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If you permit me very briefly, we indicated -- well, there are over 105 exhibits in the 65 ter list, and we believe that a large part of the exhibits actually do not correspond to the indictment. The descriptions -- actually, the correspondence of the witness to different organs regarding certain disciplinary proceedings against him are, in my opinion, quite irrelevant for the matters that we are dealing with here. There are dozens of such exhibits. There are other suggested exhibit for which the witness cannot provide reliable grounds in view of the duties that he was performing at that time. These are, in brief, the remarks that I have to the proposed material, and I modestly propose that in the course of this witness's testimony and when certain exhibits are put forward, I request that we be given the opportunity to state our objections to each exhibit as it comes up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the difficulty with that is that not every exhibit's going to be referred to in the oral evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit, Your Honours, we did make a selection of the exhibits, so I really don't know how my learned friend, Ms. Moeller, is going to conduct the examination-in-chief. So it will be difficult to state in advance what would need to be left out from the exhibit list. But they could be the following numbers, if you permit me, just one minute, please. P7628, article in the newspaper Danas published in 2005; then 5267; 2729 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel need -- the counsel needs to read the numbers a little bit more slowly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat in English. Probably it would be better and easier. P2768; P2767; P2729; P2740; P2746; P2783; P2699; P2741; P2742; P2743; P2744; P2745; P2735; P2738; P2737; P2734; P2736; P2733; P2732; P2730; P2713; P2765; P2700; P2698; P2751; P2755; P2763; P2764; P2701; that would be in the main. Also, P846, this is OSCE report monitoring and powers of domestic courts to deal with war crimes from October of 2003. I think that this exhibit -- actually, this is the same objection as is objection for As Seen, As Told. I hope that colleague of mine will add something more about this objection. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, have you not had your opportunity? I really don't like a ping-pong approach to submissions in court. You really have an order that you should adopt and complete your submissions when you're making them at one go. It's a very untidy process otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but since my learned friend Mr. Visnjic spoke before me and he spoke quite generally and said that during the examination-in-chief we will use our opportunity, I didn't say everything all at once; and then you asked my learned friend Mr. Cepic to actually list the numbers. So I just have one thing to add. This is P828, it's an internal document of a non-governmental organisation, the Fund for Humanitarian Law, drafted by some lawyers. The document is called "Violations of Human Rights or Violations in Proceedings before Serbian Courts from 1998 to 2000." I think it's an internal document and it's outside of the scope of the indictment that has nothing to do with the events or with the accused here. So I believe that the document is not relevant for use. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was going to do it, but in stages. So I don't know if I should also draw your attention -- if you're already going down the list to draw your attention to the following documents: P2725 and 2781 are the same documents. Document P2750 is mentioned twice on the list. Documents P2730 and 2764 are exactly the same on the list. Document P2818 is mentioned twice on the list, and it's the same document as document P1918, which was introduced during the testimony of Witness Vasiljevic on the 22nd of January, 2007. Document P2754 is also mentioned twice on the list, and document P2744 is a document that was supposed to be -- well, General Ojdanic is cited at the bottom as the signee, but I am not sure whether he actually ever saw that document or signed it. So the context is quite unclear to me and how is it possible, if the Prosecutor can explain, that this document made it into the file. I would like to keep the right to possibly object to specific documents if the Prosecution should introduce them during the examination-in-chief as relating to our view that the witness cannot add or make comments on specific topics, in our opinion. We do not want to do that in advance. I don't want to complicate things too much by stating the objections before the proper time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you always have the right to object to a document in the context in which it may be presented, so you retain that right, obviously. Ms. Moeller, can you deal with the reference to Exhibit 828, which is said to be a report which is outside the scope of the indictment and not relevant to the accused compiled by the Fund for Humanitarian Law.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is one exhibit that was on the exhibit list from the beginning and it is one document that we referred to in our pre-trial brief, as far as I remember. The only question I would have to the witness regarding this document is whether he shares the assessment made by the OSCE on how the -- how war crime trials were conducted or not conducted. Otherwise, this is also an exhibit that would be ideal for tendering from the bar table, I think, and indeed there are some exhibits on the list that we may also choose to try to tender from the bar table, together with another number of documents relating to this aspect of lack of punishment, where we intend to file a short motion later this week regarding some other exhibits that are on the exhibit list but that I cannot and will not go through with this witness but we will seek to tender it from the bar table. This is the extent to which we deem this particular report also relevant and of probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And on what basis would he be able to share the assessment made by the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: He has been living in the country and he has as a professional military lawyer, of course, followed what happened to the cases after he left Kosovo. And I think he can give his impression of how many war crime trials have really been held ever in his country and what are the major problems connected with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, these sound like matters of fact of which he may have knowledge. But to comment on an assessment made on what sounds like a much more far-reaching investigation than any he has conducted sounds like asking him to express an expert opinion without proper foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, maybe I wasn't really clear. What I tried to say is that the OSCE report refers to the fact that there were only so-and-so ever many war crime trials ever led in this country, and I would ask him whether according to his knowledge there are any others that are not mentioned in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is an entirely different question from the one that you suggested, and therefore that I think would be an admissible question, subject to -- obviously to any particular point made at the time it's posed and the particular circumstances in which it is posed. Mr. Cepic has given a very long list of documents that he says are of questionable authenticity. How are we going to deal with them?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, we -- we can -- we have, of course, the information how we got into the possession of these documents, and as I mentioned, some we received from the State of Serbia, some we received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do they fall into a category where you would be making a submission for their admission from the bar table, in which case they can be dealt with there; or are they documents which we have to deal with in the course of the witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The -- I submit it would be of use to deal with some of them in the course of the witness's evidence because they are responses that came in in regard to particular cases he mentions in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, one -- I didn't know that's what they were, but one, for example, the very first one was a newspaper article and you know our attitude to them. So I got the impression that perhaps were documents in there which -- to which there might be a legitimate challenge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I selected -- I see your point, Your Honours, and I was mindful of that. I selected one or two newspaper articles where the witness was actually the author himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's entirely different, of course, yeah. If -- so what's the position then if you lead your evidence and a document in that list from Mr. Cepic is not specifically referred to, how do we deal with its admissibility?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, I would submit that the Defence, as Mr. -- my learned colleague Mr. Visnjic said, has, of course, the opportunity to challenge each document as I address it and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm talking about the ones you don't address. How do we deal with them if they happen also to be on Mr. Cepic's list?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I don't address them, I will not seek to tender them through this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- so there is no dispute between the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. So you would seek to tender them by a written submission if -- if you wanted to use them at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, but very few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: If I may just explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you need to. That's very helpful. If we know that it's only the ones referred to in the oral evidence that you seek to tender subject to making a written submission for others that you choose to tender that way, then that's fine, it gives everybody an opportunity to take exception to any one in particular as they're raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. And the reason, Your Honour, and the reason why some are on the exhibit list is that, depending on the cross-examination, it may become necessary that I seek to use some of them in re-examination. That's why I put them all on so everyone's at notice, but that is the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The -- number 846, then, the OSCE report which is said to be like As Seen, As Told, now, I don't -- or is it part of As Seen, As Told?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It's a report that was done by a special project group of the OSCE --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. We can deal with it when we come to it in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that leaves -- just one moment. And you've very helpfully been told which items have been repeated, so there's just a couple of matters we need to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it, Ms. Moeller, you accept that the right time to have applied to add the August exhibits would have been when you applied to add the witness. I just want a yes or no to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: With all due respect, no, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. That's -- well, amplify the no, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The witness at the time gave us a small amount of documents which were little bits and pieces, and they didn't allow us to have the full picture, which is why I sent a number of RFAs to get the context documentation of that. And that we only got, as I said, a dribbling in until January this year. So to put the documents of the witness in context, I needed to have these other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: At the time it would have been too early to apply to add them, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, we will allow the 65 ter list to be amended to include all the documents referred to, subject to the situation where adding them is unnecessary in one instance because the document is already introduced, that's 2818; and subject, obviously, to deleting one of those where the same document has two separate exhibit numbers; and subject also to the fact that some of them are twice in the list but have the same number. I think there are two where there are two numbers, and that must be clarified at some stage in a filing made. Mr. Visnjic identified these for you. The -- there have been a number of challenges made to either the relevance or authenticity of documents, but it's clear that in -- where there's a particular point to be made. That can be made in the course of the evidence, since the opportunity will be there when the document is identified for counsel to raise that objection. In a general -- just one general comment on the relevancy of certain documents mentioned by Mr. Cepic, it does seem to us that in principle documents relating to disciplinary proceedings against the witness himself would be relevant to a consideration of the witness's credibility and reliability. So we're unlikely to be sympathetic to that objection. That's not to say that you shouldn't raise it if you feel there is a particular point to be made about particular documents. But in general, documents about steps taken against a witness himself would appear to be relevant to an assessment of the witness. So far as the report itself is concerned, we accept that this witness is a witness of fact. It may be, on certain occasions, difficult to disentangle the fact of what might be arguably an expression of opinion. I think we're capable as professional Judges of carrying out that exercise and it didn't seem from Mr. Aleksic's submission that it was a very extensive problem. So we're alert to the problem and assure you we will attend to it as and when it arises. I think that deals with the issues which have to be dealt with at this stage, so we can now have the witness in court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have been dealing with a number of preliminary issues, but these have now been attended to and we can proceed with your evidence. Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. We have your statement and an attached document which we've read. We know that there are many other documents that will be referred to in the course of the evidence. The procedure we follow here in these circumstances is to go straight to an oral examination by counsel involved in the case, and the first counsel to ask questions of you will be for the Prosecution, and that is Ms. Moeller. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Lakic Dorovic is my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I have a degree in law and I was an officer in the law department of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what is your rank in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I am a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in which position are you currently working?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm currently head of legal services within the operative forces command. I am head of the so-called legal department or legal services.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how many years have you been working so far in the legal services of the Army of Yugoslavia, approximately?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: 25 years and three months.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, have you given a statement to representatives of the Prosecution office of this Tribunal in August and September of last year?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when you came here last week, did you have the opportunity to read back the statement that you gave then?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you inform us of some corrections that need to be made in relation to your statement?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were a few.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could the usher hand the statement to the witness, please. Your Honour, this is Exhibit 2671.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And is it correct that you made a correction in relation to paragraph 3 in relation to the word "public defence counsel" which is used there?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I wanted this term to be precise, and I said that this was a military defence counsel before military tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you also make a correction in relation to paragraph 10 where you refer to some Albanian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that these were not conscripts serving their compulsory military service, but rather, soldiers belonging to the reserve forces and those who would be sent to serve in the army as recruits in the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Then in relation to paragraph 17 of the statement, did you advise us of the first name of this first Tijanic who was mentioned in this paragraph and what is it?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tijanic's name is Milovan. I provided that name in August and September when I had my first interview with the investigators of the OTP. I also provided them with his nickname. He is also known as Mica. And I also specified that the military post was 9550 Pristina. On that occasion, this was either lost in translation or something to that effect. So on this occasion I just added this information. I said that this was Milovan Tijanic, I said what unit he was a member of and what he did during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 24 you also had a clarification to make, and I think it was concerning the sentence: "I then requested the head of the Pec police, the commander of the Pec military sectors, and others to be interviewed." What is the correction that you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: This is the military district of Pec. The case in question happened in that territory, in the territory of the Pec military district. With my previous experience, I knew that a written request was much better than an oral one. Whatever is being requested or is being issued as a task either to the military police or the security organs should be in writing, because there is always a written trail, a document. My experience told me that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: That a telephone or a similar way was not so good. At that time it was very difficult to establish telephone contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Here I wanted to specify that I asked from the authorities --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you just clarify what was your request, because I think what you requested is reflected wrongly in this English version, at least. Did you request that these people you mentioned are interviewed or something else?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Not only an interview that is conducted with the security organs or the military police. A number of other investigative procedures had to be carried out. Possible witnesses had to be approached; the superior officers had to be interviewed, those who at the time controlled the situation between Pec and Decani, in order to establish whether the persons who were mentioned, and I'm referring to Stosic and Colonel Miodrag Djordjevic whose names were mentioned in the statement. In other words, it should have been verified whether they were at that place at the time and, if they had been, what they were doing, what they were engaged in. In that way the statements that I had in the file could have been verified, and according to these statements, these two and the groups of soldiers as well as a group of civilians, all of them together participated in the expulsion of a group of Albanian civilians consisting of some 700 persons --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- that they kept them --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We will go in the details of this incident later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm certainly not clear what change you want to make to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. I understood - and maybe I can ask the witness directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In regard to this paragraph, did you want to make a change that the request to the Pec police and the military commander was that they investigate the allegations and not that they be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: An investigation cannot be carried out by a commander. An investigation is carried out by the authorised organs, and in this particular case the authorised organs were the investigative judge, who didn't do anything. That is why I, as a prosecutor, pursuant to a war decree and on the order of my superior, the supreme prosecutor, issued those tasks, because it was obvious at the time that the security organs did not want to do their job.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: This is where I would like to be precise. I was the one who provided those tasks myself in order to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's -- you're going in many details here, and I think it is not easy to follow us. Could you say in one sentence maybe or two what is wrongly said in this paragraph, if anything. Or is the paragraph actually correctly in reflecting what you said?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Not just the interview is at stake if when you say "interview" you mean a telephone conversation. What I wanted to state was that I issued written tasks; I issued them in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what do you want us to do, delete that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, I would -- I understood the witness now to say it went beyond interviews comprising full investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what matters is whether that sentence is accurate or not. So should we take it out?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You can -- we can take it out, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- and take the evidence of today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 25, you refer to a certain Milos Spasojevic, and in the last sentence it reads: "Spasojevic was in the military security service before he became military prosecutor." Do you have a clarification - and please be short if possible - to this sentence?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I know for a fact that Milos Spasojevic was cooperating with the military security. Before he joined the military prosecutor's office as an associate of the service, he was engaged in different tasks, and travelled to Kosovo together. I wanted to say that he was cooperating with the military security service, that he travelled with me to Kosovo, and that he started working as a military prosecutor. On the 22nd of May, 1999, he travelled to Kosovo; but before that, he cooperated with the military security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: This is my clarification. I wanted to emphasise the word "cooperating." He cooperated with the military security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 35 of your statement, you refer to a grave-site discovered near Orahovac. And the statement refers to 37 bodies. Do you want to make a correction to the number of the bodies; and which, if so?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: The number is 47.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the last paragraph number 48, the second-last sentence refers to the extortion of 60.000 Deutschemarks. Did you want to make a clarification who made this payment?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to say that the state, the Federal State of Yugoslavia, imposed -- paid damages to two people whom Stojkovic had kidnapped. For a while he kept them under very dark conditions, tied in chains in a cellar. Then a proceedings had been staged in order to liberate these two people. Their defence attorneys later on filed a suit for damages, and the state eventually paid 60.000 German marks to these people. I wanted to be clear and say that the -- this money was paid in damages as compensation for the damage inflicted upon two persons by Stojkovic, who was a security man at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would also suggest to delete this sentence and take this explanation instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what about the main part of the sentence: "I had indicted him," is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Only as far as the money payment is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. So after mistreating them it should be: "And rendering the state liable to pay compensation of 60.000 Deutschemarks"?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, sir, with these corrections and explanations that you gave today in mind, do you attest today that the statement you gave in August and September last year is true and correct to the best of your knowledge; and would you say the same if you were asked questions -- all these questions today?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Everything I stated, I stated as a person experienced in these tasks. I was aware of the weight of each and every of the words that I said. I spoke the truth, and if I'm given an opportunity, I can elaborate on everything that is in my statement. I can provide some specific proof to corroborate the truth of everything that I stated. If I were asked the same questions today, my statement would be absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender 2671.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does the overview of regulations have a separate number or is it --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you going on to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, did you also give a statement on the work of military courts and military prosecutors, according to the laws, in August last year?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to the prosecutors in the investigative department in Belgrade, and I provided my statement on the 15th of August. And this analysis was drafted after I had been given permission by the Government of Yugoslavia that I could testify before the Tribunal. And in the conclusion of the Government of Serbia, there were 15 issues on which I was allowed to testify. The Prosecutor's office asked me to provide a written analysis of the laws and regulations that were in effect between 1995 and 2004 and provide that analysis to the Prosecutor's office, which I did eventually.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see Mr. Cepic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I suppose that my learned friend Moeller now wants to tell us something more about document number P2672; however, the witness has mentioned his statement given on the 15th of August, 2006. But the only statement that we have was provided on the 30th and 31 August and 1 September 2006. The number of that document is 2671. However, the analysis that the witness mentions under 2672 is no statement at all. This is the analysis that has just been explained. Likewise, this analysis is something that we contest, because the witness was asked to provide an opinion about the proceedings that were conducted between 1995 and 2004. This witness is a fact witness; he is not an expert witness. That is why we contest this analysis and its relevance for the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That objection has already been raised by Mr. Aleksic, and we have already given a ruling on it. And we will abide by the ruling we've already made in relation to it. As far as the statement is concerned, that's a statement to the Office of the Prosecution in Belgrade, which is not relied upon here, as I understand it. But if there's an issue of disclosure, that's a separate matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May I explain, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This paper is the very statement we are talking about; there is no separate statement. I called it a statement because it is signed by the witness and it was given by him, and he gave this paper to the Belgrade field office because -- before we met for the actual interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- and then we discussed it in this very interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only problem I have with that is it's dated the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it is the same as what the witness says he gave on the 15th of August?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: He drafted it and signed it on the 14th and he gave it to the field office on the 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when we took the actual statement, 2671, he, in the last paragraph, paragraph 58, I think, he explicitly included his statement on these matters in his very statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're tendering that statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, very well. It is admitted on the basis we indicated initially in response to Mr. Aleksic's objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, I would now like to address with you some aspects that you deal with in the statement we just talked about, the statement on the military courts and military prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And I am wondering, Your Honours, may I give the statement to the witness so he can look at certain pages that I want him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this the August and September statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No. This is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the usher hand this, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In the Serbian version, I think it is page 8, sir, if you could look at that. And the English version would be page 22 and the following, which deals with the system during a state of war. Is it correct, sir, that these particular rules would be applicable for the time starting with the 24 of March, 1999, when a state of war was declared?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and they were applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And Article 74 of the ZBS --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And for Your Honours' information, the ZBS is the law on military courts and this is Exhibit P109 [sic], which we would also seek to tender as a background to this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In Article 74 it was ruled where during such a state of war military courts would be established. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were established and they began functioning. Actually, the courts began with the declaration of the state of war before they were already formed and organised in preparation and with the declaration of the state of war they just then actually began with their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And these military courts of first instance would be established, at the commands of military districts, divisions, corps, armies, and other places?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but when they began working, the peacetime military courts of the first instance stopped functioning. We know that there were three in Belgrade, Nis, and Podgorica. Also, under the regulations and the rules on the operation of wartime military courts, when the wartime courts began functioning on the first day, then the peacetime courts, the three that we know existed, all the cases that were still open as well as the cases that had to be archived as well as the complete documentation and all the items in the peacetime courts were handed over and this was stressed and this is how it was also done in practice to the military courts which were formed at the commands of the military district. I was a military prosecutor at the military tribunal in Belgrade, and on the 29th [as interpreted] of March my previous chief, Colonel Petkovic, who was the peacetime military prosecutor, handed over duty to me; and he formally handed over to me all the cases and all the other cases, the case files and the items that he had as the military prosecutor in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me, just correction in transcript, page 26, line 14, I think that witness said "24th of March" not "29th of March."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. That makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And while you were in Kosovo in Pristina, where -- at which military -- sorry -- military prosecutor's office were you working there? Where was this office established?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: For purposes of stating the full truth, I will say that mostly we worked in the civilian premises, thus we were -- I was -- as the military prosecutor, I actually changed seven locations. My prosecutor's office and the court before which I worked during the war changed locations seven times. Specifically in Pristina, because I got there towards the end of the war, on the 22nd of May, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, I don't think the question related to which buildings you were in. The question was whether you were in -- when you were in Kosovo you were established at the command of a military district, a division, a corps, or an army. Could you tell us that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the command of the Pristina Military District. That is the full name of the organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the Pristina Military District at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you are thinking of the Pristina Military District. It was Colonel Zlatomir Pesic at the time when I was there. I think that actually he was there throughout the whole period of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And was there also a military prosecutor established at the command of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a military prosecutor and a military court at the 3rd Army command, as well as at other armies. There was another court that was operating in Kosovo and another prosecutor's office, and that is the military court at the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And Article 74 also provides for the establishment of military courts at corps level. Was there a military court and/or a military prosecutor established at the command of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what the witness has just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just explained that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Yes. Thank you. Now, Article 75 of the law on military courts deals with the appointment of -- appointment or removal of judges, judge jurors, et cetera, and it provides for the appointment by the president of the republic on the recommendation of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. In 1999, who held the position of this Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, if Your Honours permit me, I would like to be specific about the following. The chief of the head -- the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command at the time was General Pavkovic. And according to the regulations, there was a difference as for the authority to propose candidates for judges. Candidates for judges were put forward by the defence minister, while the prosecutors were put forward for appointment to wartime duties to military tribunals, or rather, to the military prosecutor's office by the Chief of Staff of the command, who was General Pavkovic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that the system did not work the same way as the regulation provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is an exceptionally important question, and I have personal experience. I was there and I can answer briefly that in fact that was at the beginning of the work of our military courts the greatest, in my opinion, problem. What happened, unfortunately, was that appointments were given to people nobody ever assumed could be placed at such high functions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You misunderstand my question. The -- Article 75, as I read it, relates only to presidents, judges, and judge jurors of military courts; it does not refer to prosecutors. And the rule says that the person who recommends to the president their appointment is the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. Now, you've just told us that in fact the appointment of judges was recommended by the minister of defence and -- but you went on to say that the appointment of prosecutors was recommended by the Chief of Staff. Now, that seems to be different from what the regulation provides for, and that's all I wanted to be clear about. I don't want to hear of examples where you think the wrong people were put in post or anything like that. I just want to know whether the official system actually worked differently from the way in which the regulation is set out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were different jurisdictions in putting forward candidates in peacetime. There is a difference from that and the same activity in wartime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're only -- at the moment we're only dealing with a state of war. We are dealing with Article 75. You've got it in front of you, so try to concentrate your answer on that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I assist maybe and ask some questions about the specific rule regarding military prosecutors, which is also in his paper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And it is English version page 34.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in the Serbian version, sir, if you could look at page 13, I think it is. There is a reference to Article 37 of the ZVT, which is the law on military prosecutors which we have in the same exhibit number as the law on military courts, Exhibit 1309. And Article 37 also refers to the appointment but now of first-instance military prosecutors, sir. And looking at that, is that the same -- more or less the same rule as for military judges?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Based on the regulations from the laws, if you read them you can see that in either case the jurisdiction is set in wartime. The Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command is the one who puts forward candidates for appointment. The decision is made by the minister, but the judges are covered in Article 74 of the law and Article 37 of the law on military prosecutors. And that's natural because these are different laws and different state organs, so it is the duty of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command to put forward command -- to put forward candidates, and the decision in either of those cases is made by the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why did you earlier point to a difference between the appointment of judges and the appointment of prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about the difference in jurisdiction for appointment -- actually, for putting forward candidates in peacetime and in wartime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying that the recommendation for appointment in peacetime is made by the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In peacetime it was the minister of defence who put forward candidates for appointment to duties, both of the president and judges in peacetime military courts. And also candidates for appointment or for election of prosecutors and deputy military prosecutors in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, you deal in your paper also -- in your statement also with disciplinary responsibility, and in the English version on pages 43 and again with these responsibilities during a state of war. It is page 16, I think in the Serbian version. And is it correct that these disciplinary responsibilities are regulated in the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, the said VJ?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Which is Exhibit 984, Your Honours, and I think that's already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the disciplinary responsibility of servicemen is regulated in this Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, sir?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: It would be quite precise if we were to say that it's regulated in the provisions of Article 159 to 186 DJ of the law with all the amendments. So during the war, the disciplinary system was regulated by those regulations of the law on the military as well as the rules on military discipline, which were drafted by the president of the republic according to the explanation provided in one of the provisions of the Law on the Military. So the regulations of the military -- Law on Military and the regulations, all of this was published in the Official Gazette. And without being immodest, I would like to say that I was one of the draftees of those regulations as well as the Law on the Military. So those two regulations governed the disciplinary proceeding system in peacetime and wartime. The Law on the Military and the Rules on Military Discipline both contain separate sections, regulations on work and disciplinary responsibility in wartime. And you can say that the same regulations can be applied, that it's only the proceedings that are shorter and the deadlines to undertake certain measures are also shorter, in view of the natural --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you clarify for us -- you referred to Article 159 to 186 DJ. What does that mean? Which law is that?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: The Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, and these specific points marked with letters are regulations from an addition to the Law on the Military regulating differently, up to a point, the responsibility of reserve military officers. So there is nothing different, really, in these regulations pertaining to military personnel in peacetime or wartime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how that fits in. Maybe you're going to clarify it, but your reference, I assume, was going to be to Article 204.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, that would be my next question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is that -- yeah. But where do we see any reference to 159 to 186? Is it earlier or -- oh, yes, I think it is earlier. Yeah, there's very detailed references.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, there are detailed references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So really guiding us to page 43 was a bit premature perhaps. There are earlier parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyway, it's now clear. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I was going right to the discipline and wartime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- whereas details are set out in the peacetime part. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, we were talking about disciplinary responsibility. What about responsibility of servicemen for serious crimes. Where would that be ruled? Where would that be established, in which laws?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: In our country there is no separate military criminal law; there is general criminal law. And military personnel and civilians serving in the military in criminal proceedings are responsible according to the Rules of Criminal Procedure under the Law on Criminal Procedure, which applies to all the other persons in the proceedings. There is no special criminal material law; there is just one general law which applies to all. It's just a question of organisation, jurisdiction, and there are only four provisions in the Law on Military Courts which regulate in a specific way the proceedings and the jurisdiction. Everything else is under the general regulations of the criminal law of the SFRY at that time and the Law on Criminal Procedure. An exceptionally important article is Article 52 on the Law on Military Courts and it's specific also. You could say that, in essence, Article 7 of the Law on Military Prosecutors is similar to this Article 52. They both provide for the following: The jurisdiction of the police in proceedings before civilian courts in the military legal system is handed over to military security and military police, and that's how it was until the beginning of 2002 when finally, because of pressure of the professional public within the military laws and other civilian courts in the country, it was decided that our state, too, the secret police should be excluded from the pre-trial proceedings. At that point, our courts, from the aspect of the law, were given a free hand in that stage of the criminal proceedings to be able to work in accordance with the law to give assignments to the military police, which actually, from that point on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if I could interrupt, please. Let's concentrate on the period that we're most interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And to take us to the aspects you just talked about, the cooperation of various organs in the pre-trial -- in the investigation and pre-trial phase, you also dealt with the responsibility of superior officers in your statement. That is pages 59 onwards in the English version. And you say that military officers and superior officers have a significant role in the pre-trial phase and they have significant duties and powers. On page 60 in the English version you refer to the organs of military security and military police, and there is a reference to Article 52, item 3, of the Law on Military Courts. In -- sorry. In the following pages you set out, then, the difficult -- the different obligations that exist regarding the arresting of perpetrators, duties during proceedings, and so on. Now, I understand these are the legal duties. How did this work de facto?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, my experience tells me that it was not applied. When I worked as a military prosecutor during the war, as a military prosecutor in wartime, in Belgrade and in Kosovo, and before that as the deputy military prosecutor, and generally as an expert associate at the supreme military court, I responsibly state that I am not aware, I had no single case in which the military officer used the authority given to him by law in respect of a perpetrator of a specific criminal act, even though I know that there were many cases in which he not only could have but was also obliged to do so under the law. For example, the company commander is responsible and should -- if he finds a perpetrator in the middle of committing an act, he's obliged to arrest him, and in that sense he's equal to an authorised person from the police or the military police, so civilian police or military police. And I responsibly state that in my practice that authority was not used once. So the authorised military officers mostly did not do something like that. Unfortunately, they handed that duty over to members of the military security organs, and I must stress that military officers complied mostly with all the tasks handed over to them directly by the prosecutors. If it went past the military security organs, then they did comply, and that is my experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can I ask you for a clarification. In your statement you say --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And that is page 60, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: "It is stipulated in Article 61, paragraph 1 of the law on military courts that a superior officer is required to take steps to prevent the perpetrator of the crime that is being prosecuted ex officio from going into hiding or escaping." I am not quite clear, what does it mean the perpetrator that is being prosecuted ex officio in this context?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I assume that in other legislations also no crimes are prosecuted ex officio. In our law there are such crimes which are either subject to private lawsuit such as defamation or similar crimes. On the other hand, there are, however, such criminal acts that are detrimental to society, and we're talking about most of the crimes under the criminal law of Yugoslavia, and such criminal acts are prosecuted ex officio. All acts of crime described in chapter 20 against the Army of Yugoslavia are acts that are prosecuted ex officio. All acts against constitution and security of the state are also prosecuted ex officio. All crimes that might be of some interest because of their gravity are prosecuted ex officio.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So serious crimes like murder or crimes against international law would be falling in this category of ex officio prosecutable crimes?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a very broad, leading question about crimes under international law which are not necessarily crimes within other domestic jurisdictions. Are you telling us that that was the position in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and there is a specific law which I will come to in a minute which deals with particular obligations of military commanders in respect to these crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. I was particularly concerned by the leading nature of that question, but if it's well-justified, that's different.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we can move on to this particular aspect right away so we can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: On page 66 of your paper in the English version, you refer to regulations on the application of the rules of the international laws of war in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just a page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I see Mr. Cepic on --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Could we have a page number in B/C/S, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Maybe the witness can help because I don't have the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 25, the last chapter in the document on page 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You say these regulations entered into force on 10 June 1988. Were they still in force in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: They're still in force. Together with my then-chief I worked on the drafting of the instructions and the rules applying to international laws, and we distributed these regulations to all units. This is a very well-drafted booklet which was printed in quite a large number of copies. And there is also an instruction on the implementation of the rules and an instruction outlying all the obligations. They're still in force. They were passed in 1999, but they are still being --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction: 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they are still in force. Article --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought it was 1988 and the interpreter is telling us 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you clarify, please, sir. In your paper it says "1988."

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: 1988, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you refer on page 67 English version to item 21 which deals with the responsibility for the actions of subordinates. Would it be -- is that a more specific rule regarding responsibility of superior officers for these particular crimes than the general rule we looked at before or how is the relationship between the two?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Item 21 of the regulations on the application of the international laws of war in the armed forces of the SFRY prescribes what is today known as command responsibility in both the theory and practice of those. Dealing with responsibility of the superior officer, in the law we have a very specific definition of a higher officer and a superior officer. The notion of a superior officer is defined by other regulations, and here what is defined is their criminal liability in case they don't take certain measures if they know that their subordinate or subordinated officer is preparing criminal act and if they admit to carry out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, we can read what it says. Can I ask you, however, one particular question. You told us that there was no separate military criminal law from general criminal law and that there were only four provisions in the Law on Military Courts, which regulate in a specific way the proceedings and the jurisdiction. Now, is this one of these four exceptions that you were talking of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, unfortunately not. The four exceptions, i.e., special provisions, deal with other things, one of them is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't need the details of them at the moment. So does that mean that this provision we're now looking at is an example of where there is a separate military criminal law, separate from the general criminal law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not how I understand this law. I regard it as complementary to our overall legislation and I consider it an integral part of our legislation. This provision is a complementary part of our criminal law, and in this provision, officers are reminded of their obligations arising from the Geneva Conventions, of their obligation to protect the victims of war, of the need to act by the rules of war, and they warn them about their criminal liability in case they are meant to undertake certain specific measures in certain specific situations in conditions of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This item 21, you say it's a rule regarding responsibility of an officer who violates his duties set out in this paragraph. Do these regulations contain any -- anything on the applicable sentences like a minimum or maximum sentence or anything alike, or where would that be regulated?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: In this item, no minimum or maximum sentence or any sentence at all is mentioned. The only thing that is determined is the -- is responsibility in case an officer omits to undertake certain measures. This instruction doesn't specify the type of sentence or how such sentence might be imposed. This is provided for by the general criminal law, and in that particular law there is some concrete acts of crime. For example, if we're talking about a crime against civilian population or murder of prisoners, this is regulated in the criminal law. This particular instruction, in my view, cannot be taken as a particular criminal law or a particular regulation. It is just an addition to other laws and regulations in the criminal law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, is this a convenient time to interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, we have to have a break at this stage. Could you please go with the usher, who will show you where you can wait during this break. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is brought in, I would like to point out a correction in the transcript that needs to be made regarding an exhibit number. It's on page 25, line 16, the exhibit number is noted there as P109. The correct number would be 1309.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in addition, the exhibit number of the rules on the application of international laws we dealt with before the break is Exhibit Number P998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the number you gave P66 -- oh, no, that's -- no. Sorry. That's wrong. That's the page number. So P998. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, before the break we left off talking about some regulations in the general criminal law, and I see in your statement that there are also -- that you address there two articles in the criminal code which also refer to violations of reporting duties of officials, and this is page 65 and 66 of the English version. And it should be in the Serb version just before the section on the Rules of International Law that we talked about before the break. You refer to Article 113 of the criminal code which deals with a violation of an official of a reporting a crime, and again this applies to crimes prosecutable ex officio only. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: In Article 113 -- actually, my comment was that an official person under that article is every person, including military officers, who are criminally liable should they fail to report a crime for which a prescribed sentence is more than five years' prison term.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: What kind of crimes would that be with that kind of more severe sentence, if you can give an example?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: In any case, those are serious crimes that pose threat to the society and with grave consequences. Those are mostly all crimes against the security and constitution of the state. Those would be all crimes pertaining to the category of war crimes or crimes against the civilian population, unlawful killings, and so on and so forth. In other words, all such acts that can be considered a serious with minimum penalty of five years. By and large, in war one can talk about all qualified types of a crime against the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you move on in your paper on the same page it is Article 235 of the -- I understand the criminal code. And this is in the chapter that refers particularly to offences against the Yugoslav Army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. Precisely so. The essence of this crime of nonreporting to the organs of prosecution is the omission of a superior officer to inform the command. The provision speaks of a crime that calls for measures to be taken immediately. In practice, a question arose about such an obligation with regard to the existence of crimes. This provision takes into account only the omission or failure to report on the event that has taken place, an event that requires the command to take certain measures. These are acts pertaining to the chapter listing acts against the Army of Yugoslavia. The protected person is the Army of Yugoslavia; therefore, the omission in question is the omission to report an event that was harmful or detrimental for the army. There are other crimes in the law, and there is also an obligation in the Law on Criminal Procedure which prescribes an obligation of every citizen, including every member of the army, to report crimes. There are also such provisions in general laws on criminal procedure and criminal law which specify that an omission to report a crime for which the penalty prescribed is longer than five years in prison constitutes a crime. In any case, in the Army of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You must tailor these answers, Ms. Moeller, to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Nosworthy has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to know does responsibility not ensue in the case of a crime punishable with imprisonment for a period of less than five years? What would happen in that case? Was there a total want of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are talking about a commander who is not a member of the military police or the security organs, their obligation to report the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, just listen to the question you've been asked. You've told us about Article 113, which requires anybody to report any offence punishable -- the commission of any offence punishable by five years' imprisonment. Now, what if it's an offence that doesn't carry that sentence, less than five years' imprisonment? Article 113 wouldn't apply, so what rule would apply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're talking about a crime that is prosecuted ex officio, then this provision specify an obligation to report every crime that is prosecuted ex officio. And let me just emphasise, these are also crimes that carry an imprisonment term of less than five years. A reporting obligation exists, and it is prescribed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case, the translation's wrong. Because it requires two conditions to be satisfied; it's prosecutable ex officio and punishable by five years' imprisonment. One has to wonder, Ms. Moeller, if we couldn't -- if we wouldn't be better reading the laws for ourselves than getting an explanation that might not actually reflect the true position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll move on. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what is the position? We need to go to the B/C/S version and find out if both of these conditions require to be satisfied. Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have in front -- does Mr. -- he has the report in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, would you read the paragraph dealing with this. It starts: "An official which pursuant to Article 113, paragraph 4, also means a serviceman who does not report ..." Could you read word for word what that paragraph says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the text of the criminal code of the SRJ at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Read what you have written. This is your document that you compiled. Read aloud to us in B/C/S the paragraph that starts: "An official which pursuant to Article 113, paragraph 4 of the criminal code ..." Just read your records to us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "An official pursuant to Article 113" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the witness could read slowly so the interpreters could interpret really precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Of the criminal code of the SFRY/FRY also means a serviceman who does not report a criminal offence that is prosecuted ex officio and which is punishable by five years' imprisonment or a longer sentence" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, just stop there. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said: "A criminal offence which is prosecuted ex officio and which is punishable by five years' imprisonment," which suggests that it needs to be prosecuted -- prosecutable ex officio and carry a sentence of more than five years' imprisonment. And a moment ago you told us that it's only one of these conditions that needs to be satisfied. It's prosecutable ex officio or punishable by more than five years' imprisonment. Now, which is the accurate version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have already specified that every citizen, including a serviceman, is duty-bound to report every criminal offence; however, a serviceman, as an official, if they omit to report a crime prosecutable ex officio, that's one condition. And the second condition that a prescribed sentence is more than five years, then such a serviceman will be criminally responsible. In the first case it is a responsibility which does not carry criminal responsibility; however, the second case does carry criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm totally confused now. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We think you understand, and further we understand and further examination on this will not assist us. We'll read the documents in due course. Please proceed to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the legal framework that you set out in your statement as a whole, did this legal framework allow for the efficient investigation and prosecution of crimes committed by servicemen?
