And if you can give a short answer, and I'm just talking about the legal framework as such at this point.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: The provisions of the law in themselves provided the necessary conditions; however, in practice it didn't happen simply because even graver criminal acts were not reported --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop there. You were only asked the first part of that question -- I think I need to explain to you what happens in our procedure that you don't seem to understand. And I'm sorry that I perhaps didn't explain it at the beginning. The counsel will ask you questions, and they are -- these questions are deliberately framed so that you should concentrate your answer on the question that's asked. Now, the question that you were just asked is a good example. You were only asked if the legal framework was a satisfactory framework for dealing with offences, and the answer to that is: Yes. It's one word, according to what you've just said. And you weren't asked to tell us about how it worked -- you were not asked to tell us how it worked in practice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that -- if you can concentrate on the particular questions, we'll make a lot more progress. Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And, sir, continuing with that, this very framework that you said was efficient, would it have allowed for the investigation and prosecution of crimes committed by army members in Kosovo in 1999, if there were any such crimes? And again, it would be a yes or a no answer, please.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I now would like to move on to your --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- about leading questions, and I think that the previous two questions from my learned friend, Ms. Moeller, I think that the last two questions were leading questions. So just to underline that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I disagree with you, I'm afraid, Mr. Cepic. We'll just continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- on the basis that these are -- there's nothing wrong with these questions in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm now moving on to Exhibit P2671, the other statement you gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And can we call up Exhibit P2780, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In your statement you say that you were a military prosecutor at the command of the Military District Pristina from 20 May to 5 June 1999. Can you look at that document and tell us, is that the document that appointed you to this position?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And can we call up Exhibit P2773, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And before you were appointed to this position in Pristina you stated that you were a military prosecutor at the command of the military district in Belgrade from 24 March to 20 May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And can we go to page 3 of the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you explain what this document is.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: This is my evaluation, military wartime evaluation, official evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And on the bottom of this page, this evaluation says that you were transferred to the 3rd Army Pristina Corps on the basis of your personal request. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was my third request. I actually asked to be relieved of duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And why did you ask to be transferred?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I was exposed to pressure, considerable pressure, from the security organs who were supposed to act in accordance with my requests. They had my hands tied and prevented me from performing my legal duties. I asked for protection from my superiors, the supreme military prosecutor; it did not materialise. They said that even they were exposed to even more powerful pressures and other things. They understood my request to be relieved of duty, and then they explained how it would be good to go to Kosovo, for me to go to Kosovo. At a meeting that was held in early May --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Tell us here. Thank you, sir. In your statement in the paragraphs 10 to 23, you describe certain events, and if you could have a short look at these paragraphs. Did all these events occur while you were based at the military district of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I am referring to the events that are described in paragraphs 10 to 23.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These are events from the time when I was the military prosecutor at the Belgrade Military District command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I would like to talk with you about some of the specific incidents you mention that took place while you were in your post in Pristina. And paragraph 24 you talk about a certain Stosic person.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And I would like to call up exhibit P2758, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In this paragraph you refer to having seen Stosic being mentioned in the statements of some VJ reservists. Did you have these statements in your own hands while you were in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received them from the military prosecutor at the Pristina Corps command, Major Spasojevic, in a case in which he asked for certain investigative asked, he asked the investigative judge. And that judge disagreed with the request, believing that they were not authorised to act, but that the case was in the exclusive jurisdiction of the court where I was the prosecutor. So that is when I got not only those statements but other documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Let us --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- in which Stosic was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let us stay with these documents now. The information that is contained in paragraph 24, is that the information that you became aware of through these statements?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Two of the reservists mentioned Stosic by name and Colonel Miodrag Djordjevic. Only Stosic is mentioned here. However, the others also talked about other people. So the two reserves -- the two reservists identified these two, Stosic and Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And the events you set out in this paragraph, were these the events described in the statements? And please listen to the question and only shortly answer.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: This was a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. The question was: Would you describe as the events -- these events, were they contained in these two VJ statements or where did you get this information from?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I had these -- this information as part of the case that I had at my prosecutor's office, criminal, legal case with a certain specific number. And in that case there were statements of these two with other exhibits. So that is what I'm talking about in that part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you have a look at the document which is on the screen, and the last paragraph states that no documents have been found regarding -- in the Ministry of Defence regarding this particular case. Can you explain what happened to this -- these statements that you saw and the case file that you just referred to right now.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: If it's true what they're informing about, that somebody hid or destroyed a file, a case file, there is a register, there is a criminal, legal case file, there are people, some of whom are prosecutors in the Nis District Court. One of them is a judge in a district court. There are people who worked, not just myself, worked as a prosecutor and who issued specific tasks. There is a case file. There is a register. So if this is correct that somebody hid or destroyed Stosic's case files, then I can explain in detail to the Trial Chamber how the security organ chief, Nesic, tried to force me to hand over all these documents to him with the explanation that the other prosecutor will take that case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have all that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Spasojevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have that in your statement already. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we call up Exhibit P829, please. This is a letter, I have to explain, that was sent to the OSCE mission by the Ministry of Defence of Serbia and Montenegro, and we seized it from the OSCE together with the report that we talked about earlier today, Your Honours. And there is mentioned a list of instigated and completed criminal proceedings attached to this letter and this is the next exhibit, Exhibit P830, which I would now call up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you permit me, I cannot find this exhibit on the 65 ter list. Perhaps it's my mistake, but I am trying my best to find it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, is it there?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I thought it was, Your Honour. Let me have a look, Your Honour. It is on page 15, the third from the bottom and the letter is the fourth from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They're certainly there in the English version, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I allowed for the possibility that it was my mistake. It's possible that the translation is wrong. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do we have Exhibit 830? Can we please have it on the screen. Your Honour, with your leave, I would also have a bundle of the Serbian version that I could hand to the witness to make it a bit easier for him to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you think it will help, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: On page 1 of this exhibit, on this list that the supreme military prosecutor provided on 9 April 2002, as the title says, there is a mentioning of a certain Slobodan Stosic under 1(A). Could you have a look at that, please, and it's Exhibit 830. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, is that the same person that you mention in -- who you mention in your statement?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say that in terms of the unit where he was serving. It says that he was serving in military district 1365, Raska. I know that Lieutenant-Colonel Stosic that I had the opportunity to prosecute as a prosecutor on several occasions actually was a member of the security administration engaged on special assignments. I met him for the first time already before the war. It was the gravest criminal charge that I had encountered as a prosecutor in my career, and I remembered Stosic who was a captain at the time from then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Please, let's stay -- try to stay focused still. The event mentioned in this paragraph, the village of Gornja Klina Srbica municipalities, would that be, to your knowledge, also a different event from the event you speak about in your statement with regard to Stosic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: If the place where the event is correct here, then it's another event. It's true that the time of the event is April. If I recollect this properly, what I had as a prosecutor in Pristina was sometime towards the end of April 1999, but not Klina, not Srbica, and I categorically state, I know that well, many others know that who are still trying cases and prosecuting today, know that this event has to do with a grave containing 47 bodies near Orahovac --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- Orahovac-Srbica-Klina, these are different locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours permit me, I would just like to say also that I had the opportunity to meet Stosic in other cases or encountered his name in other events that took place at other locations, and I said in the statement when I spoke about Stosic and Djordjevic - and we're talking about the expulsion of a group of 700 near Decani and the grave near Orahovac, those were two things that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to paragraph 29 of the statement where you refer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- is it clear in this statement that there is involvement -- alleged involvement of Stosic in relation to the bodies in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, this paragraph 35 deals with the mass grave in Orahovac and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, what is the link you are making between Stosic and the 47 bodies exhumed in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since I knew who Slobodan Stosic was and since I know that there were charges about him committing other things before this which came from the supreme military prosecutor, when I found information about Stosic and Djordjevic from those two reservists, I immediately thought that it was the same person. And I'm going to say that since this is a major thing, I called my bosses at that instant and asked General Obrencevic to check whether it was the same person and he told me at once, Yes, Dorovic, it's that same person. We know about this and we're going to order you from here what you will do next with that case. As for the grave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're only now -- you see, I wonder if you really were listening to my question. I want to know the link that you make between him and the grave in Orahovac, and you haven't even begun to deal with that yet. We don't have unlimited time in this court, unfortunately, because of the massive amount of material we have to deal with. So it would help us if you would concentrate on the questions you are being asked. So what is the link you suspect between Stosic and the mass grave in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the statements of the reservists, Stosic organised at that place as well liquidations, group liquidations, and then also the removal of bodies. So they said that he, Stosic, just like Colonel Djordjevic, did the same things in other places. I intended to take Stosic as an organiser of those liquidations. If you permit me, Your Honours, actually, it's about a larger number of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Just stop there. That -- I just wanted to know what the link was. I don't think it's in this written statement and I'm just -- I'm trying to make sure we don't miss anything as we go along. I mean, the suggestion is that this would have been dealt with in paragraph 35. Is that right, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There is a reference to many official notes that he received in this file. I don't know whether this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what he's saying is that in the statements of the two reservists there was reference to this. Anyway, move on to the matter you are going to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 29 of your statement you refer to an incident where a certain person named Nesic threatened you and asked you to withdraw indictments against two servicemen, Ristevski and Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we call up Exhibit P2754, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would like you to look at the -- at the third paragraph - it is in the English version on the first page - which starts with: "I also informed him about other forms." Can you explain what that document is shortly, if possible, please.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: There is not enough time. I would like to say that on the first evening as soon as I arrived I was put under pressure by my -- Major Nesic. From that moment until my departure from Kosovo, I was continuously --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. Try to listen to the question. Did you sign -- did you write this document?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I personally delivered it to three addresses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And to whom was this document delivered?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: To the commander; my deputy Blagojevic, who helped in the drafting and typing of the document and specified in here as the person who drafted the document. I was the one who dictated the document. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- and I delivered it to the commander, to the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the third one?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: And the third one to Colonel Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And who was he again?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: My superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: He was my superior, the military prosecutor in the department with the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I requested protection from them as well as from General Obrencevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And that was on the 30th of May. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the year is 1999 in the Serb version, is it?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Just, there is a mistake in the English translation, Your Honours, it says 1990, just to point that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Looking at the third paragraph, is that the incident that you set out there which read -- which you described in your statement in paragraph 29?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: This is exactly what I had in mind, but there were other situations which are not contained in this paragraph of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- and here I'm talking about that threat as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: To the threat --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- that was issued in front of 60 or so people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Please let us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I be clear on who the three people were to whom this was sent. Just tell us in simple language the three people you sent this to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of the military district, Colonel Pesic; the security organ of the military district in Pristina, Lieutenant-Colonel Cvijovic; the third copy was delivered to Colonel Radosavljevic at the first occasion. He was my superior officer while I was in Kosovo; he was my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And after you sent this information to these three persons about threats that were made against you in relation to your work, what happened? Was anything done to improve the situation for you?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there were just promises and encouragements that I should be brave, that I was sent over there because I was brave, and this is what it was expected from me to find ways to operate. However, immediately after this, upon General Obrencevic's order I called a meeting. The collegium of the military prosecutor that decides on the issues that have to do with the regulations of the work of the military prosecutor's office, General Obrencevic, to my astonishment, insisted on things being very formal and I needed practical assistance in acting in a very specific case. Nesic asked my deputies -- actually, he was designated as a person who had organised theft --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- in companies --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, please. This already brings us into another area. Once again, I would really ask you to focus on my concrete question and limit your response, because as the honourable Judges have expressed several times, we only have limited time and a lot of material to go through. So please try to focus on my concrete questions here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we call up Exhibit P2760, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In paragraph 31 of your statement, you state that you did not have a chance to conduct the investigation any further after that. So what was the last state of the case against Ristevski and the other person when you last saw it in Kosovo? Were there only crime reports? Was there an indictment? What was the procedural state at that time?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of May, when I arrived, the indictments had already been issued and it was signed by my predecessor. I learned about the indictment because Nesic came and asked from me to give up on criminal proceedings on that very moment. He came into my office with three soldiers armed to their teeth, and he told me, This very moment I ask you to -- there are numbers of these indictments and --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in your statement. The Judges have read your statement, and we know these details. So my question was about the status and you said there were indictments that were already signed by your predecessor. Right. So I would now ask you to look at page 3.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: They were accepted by the court. Two indictments were issued and accepted for proceedings by the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please look at page 4 of the exhibit that is now on the screen, and that was a request sent by the Office of the Prosecutor inquiring into this very case against Ristevski and the other person, Stefanovic. The third paragraph from the top says that: "The Ministry of Defence found no information that a criminal procedure was launched and led against the person named about the issues contained in our request," which are the issues you described in your statement. Do you know what happened to the indictments after you saw them in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what happened. I left Kosovo on the 4th of June, and if this is true, then somebody must have destroyed them or concealed them. These indictments are something that the court was familiar with -- actually, they were registered in the court, they were registered in the prosecutor's office, so many people knew about them. In that case, the ministry untruthfully informed -- I don't know why; I can't go into that. I know that the indictments exist. I know their numbers. I know when they were issued. I know what crimes the persons were charged with. So I really don't know how --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- how come the ministry provided such information because this information is simply not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, in a situation like this, do you also tender for admission the RFA itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would tender it as a complete package, so it's actually understandable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So does P2760 include the RFA?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, it includes the RFA and the response. All exhibits relating to RFAs include the full package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I see Mr. Visnjic -- no? Okay. May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, one more question regarding paragraph 30 in your statement before we move on. You mentioned there a certain person named Vujisic. Who was that or who is that?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Vukojica Vujisic was the previous chief of the organ in the Pristina Corps, the security organ that is --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- according to Nesic's information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Don't go into the details of what is in the statement, please. I just wanted to clarify who he is because this is not contained in the statement. I would now move on to paragraph 35 which deals with the grave-site in Orahovac which we already discussed shortly today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: If we could call up Exhibit 2761.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You say in your statement that you had to hand over this file to the military prosecutor Spasojevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Correct. The Supreme Military Prosecutor General Obrencevic ordered me to do so, and the same order came from my immediate superior, Colonel Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And if we now could look at page 4 of the exhibit which is now displayed. The second paragraph refers to forwarding of a file on 2nd June 1999 from the prosecutor within the command of the Pristina Military District to the office within the command of the Pristina Corps. Do I understand correctly that this is exactly what you described in paragraph 36 of your statement, that this was this transfer of this file?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly that, the transfer of the case file to Prosecutor Spasojevic, from the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Now --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: This is where I explained that I'm doing it on the orders of others against my will, because at the time and still today I believe that this was within my authority --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have all that in your statement. Please treat us as knowing what it is we want from you. Allow us to control what's happening in this courtroom, please. You may be used to a different system, but I think I've explained to you a number of times that you are here to answer specific questions because we already have bundles of material from you. Now, please listen to these questions and confine your answers to what you are asked. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, there is another sentence in this paragraph, in this document, a bit down -- it's actually the last sentence in this very paragraph, which says that: "The Ministry of Defence informed that it is not in possession of the documentation...." of this case, and according to what you say in paragraph 35, there was quite an extensive documentation. You refer to notes and reports and other things that were in the file. You say it contained 150 documents. My question to you would be: Where would this file be?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't know. I really don't know. The case file existed. I had studied 150 documents in the case file. The case file had been given to me by Lieutenant-Colonel Spasojevic. I consulted my superiors. They ordered me to return it. I don't know what happened to this case file.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to say that this was all registered with the court, with the prosecutor's office. I really don't know what happened to the case file in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Another case you referred to is dealt with in paragraph 34 of your statement, and it concerns a network of people who were looting Kosovo Albanian shops and enterprises and transporting the goods to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we don't -- we may call up the exhibit, but I may inform you beforehand that Exhibit P2796 is a request that we sent in this regard to Serbia on the 14th of September, and we sent a reminder on the 18th of January this year, and there is no response we received. We would tender it on this basis and apply to submit any response we receive as we receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 32 of your statement you refer to the time when you arrived in Pristina as a military prosecutor on 22nd May, and you refer to some stolen items that you saw in a Serbian house there and other things. In paragraph 36 of your statement you refer to the prosecutor who arrived with you, Spasojevic, driving a confiscated car while in Pristina. My question is: Were you ever offered any confiscated cars after you arrived in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I was threatened that if I did not accept at least one of the three that I was offered, together with all of its accompanying documents, this would be a precise answer. And they also told me if I didn't want them I could give them to anybody else I wanted to. And I would like to say that my deputies, all of them drove Siptar cars. I had a problem because I had forbidden them to drive them, and I told them, A prosecutor cannot be allowed to drive a stolen car. Spasojevic drove one. I told him that this was not nice, and later on I even filed a criminal report specifying all these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This may be a translation problem, but you started that answer by saying: "I was threatened that if I did not accept at least one ..." but you did not tell us the nature of the threat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, one of the three, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What were you threatened would happen if you did not accept at least one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We arrived on the 22nd in the evening --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just tell me what the threat was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told me that he didn't need a prosecutor of that sort, and he also told me that I would be chased away or killed. Nesic told me that in front of four people in my office. He told me he did not need a prosecutor like that, and at dawn I was given the documents for all these vehicles. And Nesic told me, Take this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- don't play with your life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Clarifying this a little bit, you talked about confiscated cars and then you called them stolen cars, and you also referred to some documents that came with the cars. What was the procedure how these cars were actually taken from Kosovo Albanians? And I mean de facto.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: One of my deputies, the current judge of the district court, on several occasions said that he had expelled a neighbour of his to Istanbul. He took his car and he said on several occasions that this was the best car that could be found in Pristina. Major Markovic, the secretary to the commander, claimed that he maybe had even a better car that he had also taken from an expelled Siptar. All of them, to the last, all of my deputies, drove not just one but several such cars. Some of them even had up to four confiscated Siptar cars. I'm claiming that they drove them to Serbia and kept some of them. The current judge and the then-prosecutor also kept a car. I can give you the number of the registration plate, the number of chassis, and all other people know these things as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, was Nesic the commander of the security organ of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at the time when I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In times of war, is there a legal opportunity to confiscate vehicles and other items if the army needs such?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: In certain situations, according to the Rules of the International Law, if such vehicles may be of use to the units engaged in legal military activities, then the answer would be yes. However, these vehicles were not taken in such situations. In Pristina, the only thing that existed were unit commands. These vehicles were taken away from the Albanians that had been expelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. You already explained that.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- the property that was left mind was just confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And if a vehicle would have or would be confiscated under the laws, which -- are there laws that regulate what happens with such vehicles once the army does not need them any longer?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: They should be returned, but the term "confiscated" is not very precise. The term that I would use would be "stolen by force" or "taken away" --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No. Please listen. I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- or "seized by force."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- the legal procedure. Is there a law that regulates the rights or the claims that the owner of such a vehicle would have? Is that regulated by any law?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And do you know which law that is?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, in civil law -- this is a law on obligations that imposes the requirement on the person to compensate the aggrieved person, and if the perpetrator is not known, then the state is obliged to compensate the person who suffered consequences. There is also the criminal code that talks about the confiscation of property -- actually, about property that were obtained through a criminal act or intended for a -- the perpetration of a criminal act. If arms were used to seize such property, then we're talking about an aggravated robbery and such property has to be returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you really -- I wonder if you really mean to say "confiscation of property" or whether this is an interpretational problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in our law previously existed a penalty called "confiscation from the convicted person." When I am talking about seizure, I don't mean to say "confiscation" because confiscation is something that follows a decision by a state body, by an authorised state body. In this case here we should use the word "seized" property rather than "confiscated" property from the citizens of one's state in one part of that state under the state of war or even before the state of war was proclaimed in the second part of 1998 when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You already mentioned that you filed a criminal report about these issues at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we call up Exhibit P2725, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could you look at the first paragraph -- or first of all, could you tell us, are you the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I was the one who filed this report to the supreme military prosecutor, because I knew that it would have been pointless to send to those people down there. I wanted to be certain that this would be taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph you refer to 15 case files which deal with -- with -- also with vehicles that were taken away, is that correct, and then you give -- in the second paragraph you give some examples, do you?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That's how it's written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that if the Prosecutor read it correctly I think it's 17 criminal and legal cases, not 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, it mentions 17 in the first and then 15 which refer to particular items.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In any event, sir, you give a lot of information on these issues on seized cars, but also you mention other cases. On page 3 in the English version there is again a mentioning of the Ristevski and Stefanovic case which we discussed earlier today in court.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those are the two indictments, and that's where their numbers are written, too. And I've already tried to explain to Their Honours, and they disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I assume that the security organs, or rather, this was personally handled by Nesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: They were seized and most probably destroyed, since later there is no information that these indictments were actually proceeded upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: If the court permits --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- please, because I want to ask you something specific. This criminal report concerns these 17 cases that you refer to in your statement as having been stolen or disappeared from the court in Pristina. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Disappeared. It would be precise to say that Nesic with his group literally seized them and took them away. Theft is one thing. It's when most frequently this is done in the absence of the owner or the official persons, but here it was literally done by force, by using threats. Before that, he had requested for us to withdraw the indictment, to suspend the criminal prosecution; and then later he took those two indictments and 17 investigation cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. It was 70 [sic] files altogether, was it, because now it -- I understand --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: 70 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we be assured we don't have a translation difficulty here, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question of the Prosecutor and the response mentioned 17, 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would like to move on now to paragraph 40 and onwards in your statement relating to the same issue, namely the cars that were taken by the army while in Kosovo. In paragraph 43 of your statement you refer to a note that you drafted in preparation for a meeting that you were ordered to attend on behalf of your superiors?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we call up Exhibit 2751, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you have a look at that document. Is that the note that you refer to in paragraph 43 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- has my handwritten remark on that -- of that day. Yes, that is my official note.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you deliver this note to the participants of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the approval of the supreme military court, General Milos Gojkovic, he previously initialled in the upper right-hand corner, he approved it personally. When I came to attend the meeting at the General Staff, since I was a representative of the military system, legal system, and I was representing military prosecutor's office, in accordance with the order of the presiding judge of the court, I distributed this note to all the participants. I think there was about 30 of them. They were mostly all representatives of organisational unit of the General Staff and the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now I would like to look at Exhibit 2752.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And this is a table, now we have it in English as well, called: "Overview of confiscated and seized motor vehicles." And where -- where does this table come from?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: It's a table of -- it's a table that I was given by General Obrencevic and General Gojkovic, and they had it at two previously held meetings. However, we received the same table at the meeting held at the transport and traffic administration of the General Staff. It was a meeting conducted by General Uzelac, and he personally ordered these tables to be distributed to all the participants, but I already had a copy on my arrival at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And can you explain in the left column in English it says: "1st Army, 2nd Army, 3rd Army." If you look at the numbers, the total numbers, at the very right-hand side, that number of 1.333 total cars, would that be the number of confiscated and/or seized motor vehicles from Kosovo or what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it can be taken like that, although it says the 3rd Army, the 3rd Army was deployed in -- throughout a large part of Serbia. But in view of the topic of the meeting and of everything else, I assert that these were vehicles from Kosovo, even though in the table it's indicated that is a overview of confiscated vehicles in the 3rd Army. The 3rd Army was outside of Kosovo; only one part of it, the Pristina Corps, was there, units that were part of the defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, would you look at the heading of this document, and could you read the heading, please, to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian it says: "Of confiscated and seized motor vehicles," "zaplenjenih." I already said that confiscation can imply a decision of the state body, state organ. I personally believe that a decision on confiscation is reached at a lower level than the command level. I am not aware of anyone really issuing an instruction for vehicles to be confiscated and taken out of Kosovo. But it's a fact that this was done and it's a fact that we noted at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind us what in law would be a justification for confiscating a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said that the use of units, according to Rules of International Law, there are situations when it is permitted in the field to confiscate a vehicle and to use it. That's it. But in other situations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I'm having trouble with. I would not, in ordinary English use of language, regard that as confiscating a vehicle; I would regard it as requisitioning a vehicle for military purposes, and the word "confiscation" is causing me difficulty. Can you assist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Bonomy, I think the most appropriate term would be "use for military purposes." Since I worked for a long time in the section that drafted regulations, we would define special-purpose use of a vehicle. But this is not in question here. When it was done for that purpose, then it would be adequate to say "use for military purposes." But this is not that kind of use, that kind of situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in that case, what is this situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that in Serbian the most adequate word, if we used one word to indicate this, it would be the word "theft," "seizure."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why would the VJ compile a document of property that they said had been stolen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because at that time there was a problem about what to do with such a large number of vehicles which were being brought there in the name of Serbia and the army by security organs, mostly the military police. Mr. President, Your Honours, this is just a small part, perhaps only a percentage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This overview relates to, I assume, the whole of the then-FRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not at all. I'm going to state that those vehicles had disappeared also, all trace was lost of them. Those vehicles were no longer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I'm assuming that the document you have in front of you relates to the whole of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, not just to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why would -- give me an example of the circumstances in which the 1st Army could have seized, other than for military purposes, 92 private motor cars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can give you a thousand actual examples that I worked on of security organs from the 1st Army, for example, from the Novi Sad Corps, organising --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll be happy with one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 10.000 vehicles were transferred in an organised manner from Vogosca near Sarajevo to Serbia. If the Court wishes, I have documents and I'm going to send them, if you wish, to the Trial Chamber attesting to an organised chain operating to obtain those vehicles. This is organised theft and the seizure of expensive cars. I worked on a case of the theft of such cars such as Alfa Romeos and other expensive vehicles in the area of Dalmatia and then also Knin and then around Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hope that perhaps later in cross-examination this may become clearer than it is at the moment. We need to break now for lunch. We will break for about an hour. Again, Mr. Dorovic, if you would please go with the usher; he will show you where to go while we have this break. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.50 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, Ms. Moeller will continue with her examination. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we call up Exhibit 2750, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Who drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I drafted the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And please --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: It was signed by the court president.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. And please wait for my question from now on again. Can you explain what this document is.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: This is the opinion of the supreme military court, since it was drafted after several meetings, on the topic of how to treat the seized or stolen vehicles, which at one point happened to be at the General Staff. So this is the position of the military -- the supreme military court and the supreme military prosecutor, I would like to emphasise, because in the debate which preceded this document and this opinion, the prosecutor and the supreme military court discussed the topic together. And I tried to evade this duty, but my generals actually forced me to prepare this document with the explanation that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, please let me interrupt you there. If you look at the second paragraph from the bottom on the first page in the English version it says: "We deem that there is no actually -- no actual need for this issue to be regulated by any special bylaw, not even in the form of an order." Why was it necessary for the president of the military -- sorry -- for the president of the supreme military court to issue such an opinion? What was he requested?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Because he was exposed to pressure from the General Staff to, through me, for the courts to help in the drafting of a document. They wanted to call it decision on how to deal with seized vehicles, but at the initial stage of the work the General Staff wanted this decision to be signed by the Chief of the General Staff and then later they wanted it also to be signed by the minister of defence. The judiciary, after analysing the question, concluded that all questions that had to do with how to proceed on the question of these vehicles are regulated by the regulations in force, and in earlier meetings as well as in the official notes -- note which I drafted too and which was presented to everyone who participated in the meetings - there were about 30 of them from the ministry and the General Staff - were told that these questions were regulated. If the vehicles were subject to criminal proceedings, then this was regulated by the Law on Criminal Procedure and the criminal code and would have to be dealt with on a case-by-case basis how a particular vehicle happened to come into the possession of the army. Since it was known that the vehicles were stolen and brought there, and since we in the judiciary knew well that all this was done by the organs of the military security and the police, I'm talking about 1.913 vehicles which were shown on the table. And we knew that it was just a fraction of what was brought from Kosovo, in fact, and from other areas, especially we insisted on it being no need -- there being no need to adopt a separate document. And the judiciary on this matter was aware of the political timing and the political climate in the country. So there's no need to refer to that here and all the reactions that could be prompted by the publication of such a document in which the army would practically make public something like that. But actually, in practice it turned out that the Chief of the General Staff --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have a clarification to seek. Now, things were regulated through this -- through this order in a general way, but what does -- how does it apply to vehicles which were not case property, I mean those which were not property of any criminal law -- of any criminal case pending? What happened to those, in reality? Were these taken away by the army or were these sold or were these distributed or what really happened? Because you have to unshroud that also for our understanding what those regulation is. Because these are, after all, forcibly taken and there can't be any regulation on a forcible taking of a property of a citizen. How would you kindly explain that, what happened, what regulation? Can you elucidate that, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly, and I am familiar with that, yes. In the work in the General Staff they pointed out that even the president of the court was driving a stolen Mercedes which was a paradoxical thing in itself, and in any event, at that time we from the judiciary mostly used the stolen vehicles to drive around in. So in the note or in the material, if we analyse it more carefully, it is discussed at one point, and this was specially analysed in the meetings, that the vehicles, until further notice, even though it is known that they were stolen, would still be used. I am well aware that some of those vehicles are being used to this very day. Sometimes when I have to go on official travel, I am actually being driven in a stolen vehicle that has been brought from somewhere. There are such vehicles that were brought from different places. It turned out in the end that the General Staff actually wanted to keep the vehicles, and that is why they insisted with us that we should deal with the vehicles in the way that is already regulated in documents in 1991, dating from 1991. These are documents in whose drafting I participated myself with the chief of the administrative department of the defence ministry, then the federal secretary, and later the defence ministry of the SFRY, which started to fall apart actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Long enough answer for us. Thank you. We must have shorter answers from you, please. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May I just clarify. These orders and rules that you just referred to regarding 1991, are these the ones you refer to in Article 45 of your statement? You were just speaking about rules that were from earlier years. Are these the ones that are set out in Article 45 of your statement so it is explained there?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those are the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And do I stand -- understand correctly that these rules were established in relation to seized items at that time? And just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Both documents originate from 1991, and the army used them whenever official records were made about the use of these vehicles in the army. They also implied records. However, lots of time has elapsed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop. You were asked to answer that question yes or no. So is the answer yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The regulations were in effect at the time and they could have been applied at the time. Both were in effect at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question related to 1991, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the question was: In 1991, when these rules were established, did they relate to items which had actually been seized at that time, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's easy, you know, isn't it? Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just for clarification to Your Honours, the document P2750 that we looked at is referred to in paragraph 46 of the witness statement. You can see the number is mentioned in paragraph 46 and this document carries the same number, so it's that very document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to paragraph 47 in your statement concerning an event in relation to Natasa Kandic. Can you tell us who Natasa Kandic is?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Natasa Kandic is the director of an NGO called Fund for Humanitarian Law. The first time I heard of her was at the time when they tried to force me to issue criminal proceedings against her for a text that had been published in August 2000. I refused to do that and then --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, please wait. We take this step by step.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Exhibit Number 2746, can we call that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you see on the screen the document? Is this the article that was -- that triggered this whole incident that is described in Article 47 -- sorry, paragraph 47 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and what you see here is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in ball-point pen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question. If Ms. Moeller wants you to deal with more, she will ask you more. All right. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In the Serbian version that you look at now there are some marks in the text, some underlining and other things; do you know who did that?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I did that when I analysed the text on the order of my superiors.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, can we call up Exhibit 2783, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see the document? In the first paragraph it refers to the text of an interview with Natasa Kandic published in the Danas newspaper. This is the article we just looked at. And it says: "For the purpose of submitting misdemeanour and criminal reports against her." This is a document that is signed by Colonel Ljubisa Zivadinovic. Who was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that at the time that his name was Zivadinovic. I believe that his name was he was Zivadinovski, but it is one and the same person. He was the chief of the law administration in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And this document was sent where, to whom?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: As you can see in the heading, it was sent to the federal ministry of defence, to the chief of legal administration. At the time this was General Radomir Gojovic, who had just been transferred from the General Staff to the ministry. And what you see here marked in handwriting above the title and to the right in the right-hand side corner is the signature as General Gojovic as the chief of administration. He says that this should be studied, that a decision should be brought urgently, and that he is giving this task to Colonel Dopudja.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That is in the handwriting which we see on the original in the right-hand corner, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now next I would like to look at Exhibit P2745.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In paragraph 47 you state that you were then asked by Gojovic to write a crime report against Ms. Kandic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: He asked me that within two hours I should issue a crime report and after that a misdemeanour report. He asked for two reports, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Okay. And then in your statement you say you refused to do that and you wrote an official note. Now, looking at the document on the screen, is that a copy of the official note that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I would like to note that I said I believe we had, I was referring to the legal administration and the ministry and this is what I did, yes, but this is just a copy because with the chief's permission I produced my opinion in handwriting, and this is just a transcript of what I had written. And this is indeed my position where the correction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that I'm not talking in singular but in plural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer to your question was yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In case there's any doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You said your original note was in handwriting and that is a typed copy of it. Who typed it up, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Dusko Dopudja who actually investigated my responsibility when I refused to issue the two requested reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you already started to explain something. Can you look at page 2, at least in the English version it is paragraph number 4. Is that how your handwritten note read as well or is there any difference?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I've already specified the difference in item 4. I was using plural, referring to all of us in the legal administration of the department. As for the rest, everything is exactly as I had written it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have paragraph 4 in English, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So the text reads: "I believe that I have more important and better things to do ..." And is that how your handwritten note read or how did it read? Just this part of the paper.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It read: "I believe that we had," not just I myself but the entire administration within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next document is Exhibit P7 -- sorry, 2743. This is a decision. Do you recognise this decision?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was shown to me on the day when the disciplinary proceedings were launched against me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And it is signed by Major-General Gojovic. You already explained who he was at the time, I think.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: My superior, my boss. He was the chief of the legal administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. The next exhibit is Exhibit 2742. This is a disciplinary investigation report, and it is signed by a Lieutenant-Colonel Dusko Dopudja. Is that the person who was ordered to conduct the investigation in these disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he did carry out the investigative procedure and also presented the results of the investigation that had been carried out. And he also proposed that in addition to the disciplinary proceedings, criminal charges were brought against me, in other words, that I was to be held responsible in both terms for having failed to issue a disciplinary report, although his personal opinion was that the disciplinary charges should not have been brought. However, General Gojovic told us that this was the conclusion of the collegium of the General Staff that met in August 2000 to discuss the alleged attacks in the media on the army on account of the army's behaviour in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And these recommendations that you should also be prosecuted in criminal proceedings, is that dealt with on page 2 in the last paragraph? Can you have a look at that. Is that the section you referred to?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: This is in the last paragraph or the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- in his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, the next Exhibit Number 2741, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This is a document signed by Radomir Gojovic again, and it is forwarding your disciplinary case file to the Federal Ministry of Defence, I understand. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: If when you say "disciplinary case file," you imply a disciplinary case, a case in disciplinary proceedings, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Now, without going in too many details, can you shortly explain to us what became out of this disciplinary case against you in regards to the Natasa Kandic article.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: In formal terms I believe that the case is still pending. That is why I was forced to at least a dozen times send requests that a formal decision should be brought and for the case to be closed. Because as soon as a disciplinary procedure is started, it has to come to an end; however, they have not been willing to finalise the case. They did not want to bring a decision from the Ministry of Defence. They came and they told me that the disciplinary proceedings were over, and then I asked them to delete that from my file, because if the case is still in the file, it might turn out that I had committed a breach of discipline or a crime. If you fail to obey orders in the army, it's considered a grave breach of discipline which might have repercussions on my career. But they would never issue such a decision. I even had to go to court, take them to court. But after the threats of the security organs, I was forced to write an article and I actually drafted in the editor's office of the paper called Blic after my meeting with Colonel Kovac from the Ministry of Defence and his men, because I had realised from that moment on, I'm facing major threats and major danger because at that meeting I pointed out to some grave breaches of discipline and crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... and call up this exhibit. We have this article. It's Exhibit 2699, the article in the Blic newspaper. If we could go to page 4, please, in the English. Do you see the document on the screen? Is that what you just referred to, the article that you wrote yourself, which was then published in the Blic newspaper?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the article that I have just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's an open letter, apparently. On what date was this written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an issue covering the period between 30 April and the 2nd of May. So this was published on the 30th of April, but it covered a longer period of time in 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And now we are in 2006 [sic]. Is there any -- has there been any decision on this whole issue in the positive or the negative since -- since it arose?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: No. The commander called me and told me not to do a letter because the case would still be on my file. And when I -- well, I have recently issued a comment with regard to the obligations of the military in respect of the Tribunal in The Hague, he again issued a decision that I should be prosecuted for the breach of discipline. I don't think it will be done, but I'm -- I still intend to write another open letter, and I told him so, and he told me that if I did that, I would be fired from service and that I shouldn't do that and before I came here he told me that I should give it a second thought and if I did go that I better not come back. I am proud that I have the professional knowledge and I am proud of what I have done in my professional career, and especially the order that I have just issued recently --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's not --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- and all of my superiors have only had the highest praise for my professional work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who is the superior to whom you're referring now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Aleksandar Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The acting commander of the operative forces, who is the commander of special forces and who was the commander of a battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: He asked another commander of the military police to carry out that investigation. I don't think that they intend to carry out that investigation, that it will ever come to anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, you just referred to the fact that your work was praised by your superiors.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we go to Exhibit 2771, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document? Is that your work evaluation for the period from 1995 to 1998?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This pertains to the time when I was deputy military prosecutor in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- I had taken over from him on the first day of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And can we go to page 3, please, in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It says on this -- in the second column from the bottom: "Conclusion of numerical grade: Excellent." Was that the overall assessment of your work? Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I always received a collective grade of excellent, and the only aspect of my work that falls short of excellent is my behaviour, because my behaviour differed from the others because I did not obey orders when I was asked to do something against the law. The person who evaluated my work is a person under whom I worked for a number of years and whose work we have analysed here today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And if we could look shortly at Exhibit P2774 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that, this is what happens. I'm now curious to know who that person was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, could you say who that person was you refer to.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Nikola Petkovic, who was the military prosecutor in Belgrade at the time, at the moment when he issued this evaluation of my work. And he also participated in writing the last war evaluation and he was the chief military prosecutor until the moment the military prosecutor's office stopped existing. I hold this person in very high esteem as a human being and as an officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said: "Whose work we have analysed here today." Can you remind me what we were analysing about his work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said that I and Colonel Petkovic drafted the laws that we have analysed today, the laws on Military Court, the military prosecutor, and bylaws necessary to implement those laws. So not the person but our joint work and we have analysed this work today here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Exhibit 2774, do you recognise this document? Is that the evaluation for your work from March 2000 to March 2004?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: This dates from an earlier period when I was in the legal administration. It was the president of the supreme military court, General Gojkovic, who wrote this evaluation for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And on page 2 your evaluation grade is stated as very good.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no. I'm sorry. This has also originated in the legal administration, but at the time when I was returned. This was Mr. Miodrag Spasojevic who was brought over from the state security of Serbia and became employed in the legal administration. He was a reserve military person who was posted to a place reserved for generals.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And last -- the second-last sentence before the stamp on page 2, if you could look at that, you already referred to that your personal behaviour was sometimes criticised. Is that what you refer to? The text refers to that you ignored subordination inter alia. Is that what you addressed earlier on today?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I had in mind. Mr. Spasojevic asked me to submit false reports, to assist him in destroying documentation. I should very much like to speak about this very specifically in what situations and concerning which documents Spasojevic wanted me to help him. This was normally the case when we were supposed to send documents or when we were supposed to respond to the court summonses from Split or to the court summonses in the country where colonels and generals had to appear before court proceedings as witnesses. This is something that they wanted to avoid at all costs. Spasojevic tried to force me, as a person who had experience in the field, to write reports that we had no such documentation, that it had been destroyed in the war. I refused to do that, even in writing, because I was afraid that what I was forced to do might incur criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And this reporting period is also the reporting period in which the incident with the Natasa Kandic article happened, is it -- is it so?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the reporting period.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, moving on to paragraph 51 of your statement, you talk about a commission that was formed in the VJ General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we call up Exhibit P2675, please, and we need page 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you have the document in front of you, sir, 2675? It should be in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I drafted the document upon the order from the chief of the administration. The representative has signed this. Since I was there at the time, Dusko Dopudja was never a representative of the chief and I can vouch for that. It is quite unfortunate that the chief of the administration dared not sign this because he was afraid of being driven out of the army; that's why he compelled this unfortunate representative to sign it, and he's merely a figurehead there. I drafted the record at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
