utterances.text: And let us please look at some text which is under VI, in the English it's on page 6. The Commission for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal which is mentioned in this paragraph, is this the same commission you mentioned in your statement in paragraph 51?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the commission. I should like to specify this as well. This is something I said at the time as well but it wasn't written down. This is the commission charged with archiving documents in the month of January of 2005. This commission consists of 23 generals --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And before you go on, could you give us some members of the commission.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: General Terzic is the president of the commission. I know that the immediate superior, General Milos Gojovic is the president of the military court and then General Svetozar Obrencevic. I see a document here bearing his initials and I know he drafted it, then the general -- the chief of the legal administration of the General Staff and then of the legal administration of the Ministry of Defence General Gojovic. Next, if I remember well, this is the person who was charged in the security organ for ensuring the security of the work of the commission, I think it's Vasilovic, I'm not sure, though. And a group of other generals whose names I might even find in my official notes. At any rate, these are the names I can think of at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 51 of your statement you say that this commission was formed by Pavkovic. Is that General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: General Pavkovic, yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- that was contained in the material we had. Because I had material showing that the commission was set up by the Chief of the General Staff. The name of the commission states that it is the commission of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: The material involved is quite voluminous and we received it from the foreign ministry. Annexed to it was a set of materials --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Please, I want to ask you specific questions regarding this document. This document is a document which was -- you say you drafted and it is from the legal administration in the Ministry of Defence; yes?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And this document deals with which issue, if you can explain very shortly and pointedly?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: From the ministry's secretariat, we received material that the ministry had in turn received from the foreign ministry. One of the documents contained in the material was the request by this Tribunal, ICTY, or that's to say by the Office of the Prosecutor, to gain -- or to be given access to the military archives of the Yugoslav Army, which also included the archives of the Ministry of Defence. Certain measures were taken in order for our state and the army to preserve their reputation and security, and this of course in the context of granting access to the archives. The commission was sternly opposed to such a request by the ICTY because it was their main task to destroy any such material, and they energetically worked toward that. There was mention of some 17.000 documents that the commission had --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... The commission, did it submit its opinion on this request by the ICTY regarding access to the VJ archives, a written opinion?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- and it exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And I have Exhibit 2684 which is this document, Your Honours. I don't want to ask any particular questions regarding this document, but it is the underlying document to the one we are dealing with at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, staying with the document we are looking at, on page 7 of the English version, the second-last paragraph - and I hope you can see it in the Serb version - reads that: "We," meaning the Ministry of Defence here, legal administration, "consider all the positions of the commission to be legally unfounded and arbitrary and as such also particularly harmful for the general interests of Serbia and Montenegro, especially with regard to cooperation with the Tribunal." One paragraph up in this document it is stated that: "In the position of the commission there is a note of cynicism and disparaging of the chief prosecutor," and you already elaborated a little bit on what in your opinion that the aim of this commission was. And very short, not going into details, and as you drafted, as you said, this document, could you explain again what this commission was set up for, basically.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: The commission was set up and organised. All the employees of the ministry were instructed that they should provide any support to the commission that they can and help it in its work. Even later on, as the commission continued working, those of us in the legal administration knew that the commission was, in fact, working toward either concealing these documents or refusing access to them to whoever sought them. It even went as far as forging or tampering with documents, changing their contents. There was a team in our administration who was charged with such activities. The commission was set up with that purpose, and it also worked along those lines in reality - let me put it directly - in concealing these documents, and if the documents could not be concealed, they worked on forging, i.e., modifying the contents of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I see Mr. Cepic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, if I understood my learned friend, Ms. Moeller, on page 95, line 6, she said that the witness participated in the drafting of the document; however, I didn't hear the witness confirm this. And as we can see, the initials next to the signature on page 2 in the B/C/S version do not include the initials of the witness sitting in the dock here. Therefore, I neither heard the witness confirm this nor could I find any evidence showing that he, in fact, drafted the document on the document itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, has that already been answered or --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm trying to find it in the transcript. To my recollection, that was the first comment he made on this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I thought, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- when it came up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I inquire as to the document referred to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at page --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at page 92, line 2; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, Your Honours. We just found it, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that good enough for you, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you remember the bit of evidence about the wrong person signing it and being compelled to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I have to underline that I'm not sure, but I think that we spoke about some other exhibit, 2675.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the one we're looking at, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, no, no at this moment we have been looking at Exhibit Number P2684.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's passed and we're back to 2675, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We made a brief departure into 2684, but we are back dealing with 2675.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'd like to move on. Can we call up Exhibit 2830, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you see the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I keep springing to my feet all the time. However, as far as I remember, document 2830 is not contained in the 65 ter list. We're thankful to the Prosecutor for including it in the list, but I have to point out that it is not in the above-mentioned list. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is. There was a mistake in the initial notification where we put the same exhibit number twice and that was this document. But we sent a corrigendum one day later on 9 March where I -- where the column regarding this document was put in and the correct ERN numbers and the correct P number was given in notice to the Defence and Your Honours because we recognised this mistake as soon as notification was filed, unfortunately not before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic says it's not there, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, the document is there in any event. The title is there. We only had wrong ERN numbers and we had a wrong P e-court number in the original notification, which was filed on 8 March. And then on 9 March we filed the corrigendum, which contains the P number and the ERNs in a correct version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went carefully through the 65 ter list, and in the list that I have there is no P2830. I was going through the list according to the P numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you'll see that it was -- that there was a correction made on the 9th of March. But do I get the impression that you're happy to see this document, in any event?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very satisfied with the document, but I'm afraid that this witness cannot provide a reliable and valid explanation or comment to that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that remains to be determined. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, could you look at the document. It's from the command of the Pristina Corps from 2nd of May. During that time you were not yet in Pristina, were you?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I was in Belgrade as a prosecutor at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, from your experience with reports and documents alike, can you have a look at the third paragraph on the -- on the first page where it lists the largest number of reports in relation to particular crimes, and then it lists murder, aggravated theft, and others. And I would like you to comment on that, if you can.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: This piece of information is very interesting. I personally know that right away, as early as at the end of March, there were many cases of murder, mass-scale murders and individual murders; therefore, it is true that there were murders. I state with full responsibility that before me as a prosecutor on the 22nd of May, that's to say near the end of the war, if we disregard the fact that we had already started working for Stosic and if we disregard the matters that could be considered as criminal reports, we started working on these mass graves. The question arose of where the criminal reports were, why weren't they there. Let me explain this closely. 1.040 criminal reports disappeared, vanished, from my prosecutor's office. I personally believe - and my bosses at the time held the same opinion - that these criminal reports, or rather, statements concerning these murders were concealed by security organs. In fact, they made a selection in the following manner. In my prosecutor's office, which was competent for all the crimes committed by civilians or any crimes involving military personnel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop. This -- I don't find this helpful at all. I can't see any relevance of this to the document in front of me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So could you take this in a way that is going to make it relevant to what we are considering.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Murder is noted as one of the offences committed and reported in the largest numbers. In relation to crime reports and investigations you saw once you arrived in Pristina later that month, if there were that many murders, were they then investigated and reported on? Did you see all these many reports? Were there reports like that or not?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I've already said this, and I repeat that under full responsibility, no, we didn't have any. And I'm speaking of my prosecutor's office and of the court I appeared before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So no murder reports; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had something I regarded as a report and we acted upon it. This was a report involving a grave-site. We had a report concerning the expulsion and attack against a group near Decani. However, in addition to the proceedings instigated against Stosic, we had no other criminal proceedings that would have originated from our prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now I would like to look at page 3 in the English version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And there is a reference to instances of concealment or late reporting of criminal offences in the units. You already mentioned several times today, you gave various examples of concealment of crimes that were committed. Now, in this document there is some mentioning of something like that, and the crimes that are listed in this paragraph in relation to which that was discovered was theft, taking a motor vehicle, looting, arson, and the like. There is no -- there is no mention of murder or anything more severe than the crimes that are set out here in this paragraph. What would you -- what would your comment be on that, if any?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: This document was drafted at the command of the Pristina Corps. I belonged to a different command, although we had direct dealings and instances of cooperation in several -- on several occasions. I can draw the conclusion that the situation was quite like this one in our office. As a prosecutor, I myself had more than 90 per cent of cases where people would evade court summons or -- these were members of the VJ. In my office, aside from the grave-site and the Stosic cases, we had no such situations. I know that the prosecutor at the Pristina Corps -- I know this because I had meetings with prosecutor Spasojevic on several occasions, I know that they had several cases involving unidentified perpetrators. These were crimes against the civilian population. That's according to what he told me. They also had several cases after mass-scale murders. Based on this knowledge, the document we have here should reflect these cases. It should also be stated at what stage these cases are. I don't really know whether the cases were perhaps brought to a close, but you can't deduce that on the basis of the document here. I don't know what happened to these cases and I don't know if I can speak about the analysis contained here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Thank you. Moving on to Exhibit 2818. This is a document of the Pristina Corps command, and it's dated 25th of May, 1999. Is that around the time you arrived in Pristina, is that?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Pristina at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And for you, sir, it's under point 2.3, the part on the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sorry, could we go to page 4, it's one page further.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In the paragraph which is just above the next headline which reads: "In the navy" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's disappeared I think from -- no, sorry. Are you back to a different paragraph? I thought it was to be paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, it starts on the previous page, Your Honour, but the particular paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- is on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The paragraph that reads: "The judicial bodies in the Pristina Military District command." This is where you were based, is it, the military district command?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was the prosecutor at that command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And this paragraph says: "They have somewhat less problems than some of the other organs mentioned in this section of the document, because the criminal proceedings and majority referred to crimes of not responding to call-up and avoiding the military service." What do you say to this assessment from your own experience?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I pointed out just earlier that over 90 per cent of what was done was for crimes from the army, and one of the two were evading duty and nonresponding to mobilisation. And these are particular things and they are quite easy to prove. So this note or this remark, in my view, is very wrong. I was sent to Kosovo just like Spasojevic, but now I'm only talking about this prosecution at the district -- military district command, just as General Gojovic said at this large meeting. It's a well-known meeting where a direct analysis was done with the military prosecutors and the military judges about the situation in the district until that moment. That was with the beginning of May 1999. And it was said that the situation in the judiciary organs of the prosecution and the chambers was catastrophic and that we should go there to try to improve things a bit better and then we were also instructed how to conduct proceeding. It was a kind of training how to respond to pressures and resist pressures from the security organs and how to force them to comply with our requests. So this conclusion does not stand. The situation was exceptionally difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, was Spasojevic your deputy in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Spasojevic is the military prosecutor at the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, in your statement in paragraphs 52 and the following, you refer to a number of exhibits that -- or a number of documents that were shown to you when you gave the statement, documents that were received in another case in this Tribunal through a Defence witness for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not intend to go with the witness through these documents because I think he has commented in his written statement on them. I would just like to give you the cross-reference to the exhibit number. The document in paragraph 52 of the statement is Exhibit 953; the document referred to in paragraph 53 of the statement is P2826; the document referred to in paragraph 54 of the statement is Exhibit P2825; and the document referred to in paragraphs 55 and 56 is Exhibit P2 -- I'm sorry, Exhibit P954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: A last exhibit I would like you to look at is Exhibit 846 --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The OSCE report that we talked earlier about, Your Honours, this morning. And if I may hand a paper copy to the witness, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, did you have a chance to have a look at this report when you came here last week?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read it, analysed it. There are some cases there that I know about from before. It's true that some cases that are mentioned and analysed here are cases that I came across for the first time, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: -- I knew about some of the cases described here from before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And from your experience, both as a legal professional and as a citizen living in your country during the time until this report was issued, which was in October 2003, do you know of any other war crime trials held in your country for crimes committed in Kosovo other than these that are mentioned in this report? And that means of course until the time of October 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know how far this question will take us, because the witness said that this is a document that he has seen here for the first time. So I don't see the point actually if my learned friend insists on getting an answer from him, but I don't really see any point in introducing this document through this witness. That is a question that she could have put to the witness without the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that can hardly be said, Mr. Visnjic, no. The witness will answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall the question?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. I do recall the answer -- the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the army at the time when I was working as a prosecutor in Belgrade, and then in the supreme military court after that, I had the opportunity to deal with the case of the massacre in Kragujevac [as interpreted], which was ascribed to an Albanian. That case is something that I and my bosses actually used to conclude that it's an unclear case. I want to be quite explicit. I think the proceedings are rigged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not mentioned -- is it not mentioned in that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not mentioned here. I wanted to say -- I've already said it, but I wanted to mention it as an example that some other cases I know about that are not mentioned here and which I had the opportunity to work on, and I can give the number of the case. I can also mention the protagonists of the security organs who took part in the setting up or the rigging of the procedure. So if the Court allows me, I can perhaps be given the opportunity to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a second. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first an objection to the transcript. The witness had said Mladenovac, not Kragujevac. Secondly, I think the witness should talk about the monitoring empowering of the domestic courts to deal with war crimes. As far as I know Mladenovac has nothing to do with war crimes if he is saying that this case does involve war crimes and if that is something that my colleague, Ms. Moeller, asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you referring to Mladenovac or Kragujevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mladenovac, yes, that is well noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the date of that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you a specific answer, but I have official documents here. I worked on that case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I want to be precise, but roughly it's from the time when I was working at the Belgrade prosecutor's office and it refers to the time when in Yugoslavia -- big Yugoslavia the war already was underway and this material talks about not only cases during wartime in Kosovo. You will see some other cases throughout Yugoslavia are mentioned here, too. So I wanted to say that I knew some of these other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Kosovo regarding war crimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you intend to pursue this, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Just in relation to the trials, trials conducted that are mentioned here in this report for war crimes in Kosovo, do you have a reason to believe, according to your personal experience as a lawyer or as a citizen in this country, that this report of the OSCE could be incomplete or not?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it is true, but to a point. The reasons for proceedings to be conducted in such a way or for it to have been processed in such a way, my personal experience indicates that there is no way, even in the foreseeable future, to resolve in the proper way the cases in order to get to the actual truth. There were even fewer proper conditions for an objective determination of the truth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the question you've been asked. The question you've been asked is whether you know of any other actual prosecutions undertaken by the authorities for war crimes committed in Kosovo which are not contained in that report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is missing here the case of the grave that I was investigating, the grave-site near Orahovac. It's not in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think I have to clarify again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This is a report about war crime trials held, trials held, not about investigations or prosecutions. It's only about the trials that were actually held and all the questions are in relation to such trials. And my question was - and maybe that's the misunderstanding here between us - do you know of any other trials that would have been held until October 2003 that are not mentioned in this paper here?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I know that Stosic and five from the group that he led were tried. I didn't notice here any mention of the outcome of that trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: There was a trial against Zoran Ristevski, against Stefanovic, Nesic was also supposed to be processed. I had submitted a request for that. They are not mentioned here. This is not referred to here. I don't know if this was not analysed or they were not known about. These are some cases that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- know about which during the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the outcome of the trial of Ristevski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nesic, the chief of the security organ, literally took the documents and he destroyed the documents about Ristevski and -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Please, you're being asked if you know of any trials which actually did take place which are not in the document. You're not being asked about things that were covered up or hidden. You're being asked what trials do you know of that did actually take place which are not mentioned in that document. And you've given one example. You say that there was a trial of Stosic and it's not in the document, and I'd like you to tell us the sentence that was imposed in that case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stosic was acquitted -- actually, the proceedings were suspended because the prosecutor had given up -- declined to prosecute further. I don't know whether it was for lack of evidence, but I believe personally that there were other reasons. I believe that there was an abundance of proof and that it should not have been suspended. I know that now after the Supreme Court of Serbia returned the case for the second time. Three of them are going to be tried now. I don't know if the trial will be in Kraljevo or Valjevo. It will be in one of the district courts, one of the two district courts. And as for two accused, again unfortunately, it seems that the prosecutor's office has declined to prosecute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, do you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that's what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know of any other examples of trials which have actually taken place which are not referred to in the document? And if you have to read it again, we don't have time for that, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall any other specific case at this point in time except for the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, you have mentioned in your statement at several points that you -- due to your outspokenness and activities, you were threatened on several occasions. Before you came here to testify, did you receive any threats?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm receiving threats continuously since 1999, and in the beginning I thought that it was only individuals who were -- felt personally threatened because of my work and the submitted charges and that they were trying to intimidate me. But as time went on, the threats were more and more serious and I understood more and more the gravity of those threats. And ultimately, I had the experience that not far from the building where I live a person who I believe did that in accordance with instructions of the military security service intercepted me and said he was going to rip both of my arms off from the elbows. And it happened that my brother, by accident, had lost fingers on both of his hands. I at that time definitely understood that there is a serious danger and that there are people who consider me to be a traitor of the Serbian cause, and at the command I had the opportunity that while I was on duty I worked with people who talked proudly about how they expelled Siptars and what sorts of things they did to them. And then when they found out that I was a prosecutor and so on, then they told me that for me the best thing would be to pick up and leave the army and to return to Montenegro. I experienced that when the two republics split apart. My superior, Colonel Sokolovic, openly called me to tell me that probably after all that I have done, I should not be thinking of staying in the service and that the best thing would be -- the wisest thing would be for me to leave. I asked for protection from the president of the republic. I sought protection also from the defence minister. My written requests were channelled to go directly via the commander. The commander did not want to pass them on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Forever or is there going to be an end to it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, there is going to be an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I want to know when was the occasion when you were threatened with ripping both of your arms from the elbows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I explained that to The Hague investigators. This was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me the date of it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in December. I think it was on the 10th of December, 2006, when I arrived from Kragujevac, where I am on duty now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now recently, actually, last weekend, last weekend when I was supposed to prepare to travel here, the same person in the same car at the same place, but the car didn't have any licence plates this time, repeated the same threats. Again, they wouldn't give me a plane ticket to get here. On the day when I was supposed to pick up my plane ticket, the commander told me that I'm going to lose my job if I previously do not receive the permission from the defence minister. So I then had to seek written permission to be allowed to come here. Shortly before I boarded the plane, the official who is checking the passports and checking the visas asked me cynically so that others could hear who were around, Whose passport is this? It was strange since he could see it was a Serbian passport. I said, well, you see it is a Serbian passport. He said, Well, I thought it was a Dutch passport. Perhaps it would have been better.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, my last question is: Against this background why did you decide to testify here in open session and without any protective measures, please?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC
utterances.text: Because I personally believe that it is better like this, that my chances are better and that they will not dare to attack me if it is known here that I testified. The Serbian press has written in detail in several daily newspapers that I have already been testifying in The Hague for four days. There are newspaper articles about it already. All of my command, 110 officers, read my request to seek protection and they know I am testifying here. They cannot extend protection to me, those who will either do what -- who would actually implement their threats. I asked for protection from those who are supposed to protect me. The military police who is conducting proceedings against me because my comment --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That would complete my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Moeller, it doesn't appear to me that P846, the OSCE report, is admitted -- would be admitted as a substantive document on the strength of the questions asked. So if you intend to seek to rely on that report, it's going to have to be presented to us with a written filing covering all the usual criteria of authenticity, relevance, probative value, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I will do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, that brings our proceedings today to an end, but that only completes the examination by the Prosecution. There will be cross-examination by a number of Defence counsel for the various accused; that will have to be tomorrow. It's important that between now and then you do not discuss any of your evidence, either what you've given or the evidence you may yet give, with anyone at all. You can, obviously, talk about whatever you like with whoever you like, as long as you do not under any circumstances discuss the evidence in the case. Now, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and return here to re-commence evidence at 9.00 a.m. tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, the order of that cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order will be: General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, General Lukic, Mr. Sainovic, and Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you have any rough estimate of its length? Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can tell you that we have a lot of material in respect to this witness, and as the matters stand at present, we will need several hours. What I'm concerned about is his extensive answers and also the way in which he arrives at certain conclusions. I will have to examine him extensively, which is not my habit of doing, and I will be dealing with matters that are more or less relevant to the indictment but are nevertheless contained in his statement. For this reason, I got cannot give you a precise estimate at this time, but if at any stage we find that we should go beyond the time the Prosecution had during their examination-in-chief, we will inform you thereof in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall resume at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.31 p.m.,
